title: The French Sentence
desc: One word is missing from a French sentence: an article, an adjective in agreement, a verb in its person, a past form, or an object pronoun. The word is chosen from tiles at the first levels and written at the higher ones.

intro.h: The article. The article agrees with its noun in gender and number, and le and la become l’ before a vowel or a mute h. An amount that is not counted takes the partitive: du, de la, de l’.
eg: le roi, la reine, l’homme, les chevaux; du pain, de l’eau

intro.h: Agreement. An adjective agrees with its noun in gender and number.
eg: un petit jardin, une belle maison, les femmes sont vieilles

intro.h: Person. French writes the subject pronoun, and the verb agrees with it in person and number.
eg: je parle, nous parlons, ils parlent

intro.h: The past. The passé composé is avoir or être with the past participle, and it presents an action as complete; the imparfait presents it as going on or repeated.
eg: il a parlé, elle est venue; la reine parlait quand le roi est entré

intro.h: The object pronoun. An object pronoun stands before the verb: le, la, les for the direct object, lui and leur for the indirect object, and y and en for a place and a quantity.
eg: le roi le voit; je lui donne le livre; il y va; j’en ai deux

items.why: Roi is masculine and singular and begins with a consonant, so the article is le.
Femme is feminine and singular, so the article is la.
Homme begins with a mute h, so le loses its vowel: l’homme.
Chevaux is plural, and the plural definite article is les for both genders.
The indefinite article before a masculine singular noun is un.
An amount of something that is not counted takes the partitive article, and pain is masculine: du pain.
Eau begins with a vowel, so the partitive is de l’: de l’eau.
After a negative, the indefinite and partitive articles become de: il n’a pas de livre.
The adjective agrees with reine, feminine and singular: heureuse. Heureusement is an adverb.
Maisons is feminine and plural, so grandes.
Jardin is masculine and singular, so petit. Petit stands before its noun.
Before a masculine singular noun that begins with a vowel, beau becomes bel: un bel ami.
Femmes is feminine and plural, so vieilles.
Livres is masculine and plural, so bons.
Maison is feminine, so belle.
Amies is feminine and plural, so contentes.
Je takes the ending -e in a verb in -er: je parle.
Tu takes the ending -s: tu finis.
Vendre has no ending in the third person singular: il vend.
The first person plural of être is sommes.
The second person plural of avoir is avez.
The third person plural of aller is vont.
The first person singular of faire is fais.
The third person plural of venir is viennent.
Parler forms the passé composé with avoir, and il takes a.
Venir forms the passé composé with être, and elle takes est.
The passé composé is avoir with the past participle, and the participle of finir is fini.
Aller takes être, and the participle agrees with ils, masculine plural: allés.
With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject, and the object comes after it, so vendu.

items.en: The queen was speaking when the king came in.
items.fr: La reine ______ quand le roi est entré.
items.why: The imparfait presents the speaking as going on when the other action happened: elle parlait. A parlé would present it as a complete act.

items.en: He used to do the work every day.
items.why: A habit in the past is given by the imparfait: il faisait.
Arriver takes être, and the participle agrees with les femmes, feminine plural: arrivées.
The direct object pronoun for a masculine singular person is le, before the verb.
She receives the book, so she is the indirect object, and the pronoun is lui.
Parler à takes an indirect object, and the plural indirect pronoun is leur.
Y stands for a place to which or in which: il y va.
En stands for a quantity of something already named: j’en ai deux.

items.en: He gives it (the book) to me.
items.why: The book is the direct object, masculine, so le, and me comes before le.
After a preposition French uses the stressed pronoun: pour toi.
The object pronoun of the second person plural is vous, before the verb.
